passage: I'm Payal, and Francis lives in the flat next to mine in Berlin. He moved from Kochi two years ago for an engineering job. In the first winter I heard him on the phone to his mother, speaking Malayalam, sounding homesick. He barely left his flat. Then I saw him at the German classes in the community centre, sitting in the front row. By spring he was cooking fish curry for our building's summer party. People lined up for seconds. He also joined a local cycling club. Last month he told me he still goes to the Kerala association once a month for Onam and songs. He said, 'I don't have to choose.' He seemed lighter saying it.

qa.q: Which city did Francis move from?
qa.a: He moved from Kochi.

qa.q: What does Francis barely leaving his flat in the first winter suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt lonely and homesick, missing his family and home.

qa.q: What helped Francis build belonging in Berlin?
qa.a: Learning German, sharing his food, joining a cycling club and keeping ties with the Kerala association.

qa.q: How does Payal see Francis's change over time?
qa.a: Payal sees him moving from lonely to settled, keeping his roots while making new connections.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a young migrant adapt to a new country while keeping his identity.

passage:
First week: Kishore moved from Patna to Chennai for work. He couldn't read the Tamil signs, and the food felt strange. He ate instant noodles in his room and called home every night.

Second month: His colleague Gurpreet, who'd moved from Amritsar a year before, took him to a small mess run by a Bihari family. Kishore nearly cried eating litti chokha. Gurpreet also dragged him to a Tamil class on Saturdays. "You'll feel less like a guest," she said.

Sixth month: Kishore could order at the tea shop in Tamil, to the owner's delight. He'd started liking filter coffee. He still missed Chhath at home, but that year he celebrated it by the Marina beach with other migrants.

qa.q: What did Kishore eat in his room in the first week?
qa.a: He ate instant noodles.

qa.q: Why did Kishore nearly cry eating litti chokha?
qa.a: The familiar food from home touched his homesickness and made him feel comforted.

qa.q: What helped Kishore feel less like a guest?
qa.a: Learning Tamil, finding familiar food and friends, and joining other migrants for Chhath.

qa.q: How might the tea shop owner see Kishore's effort to speak Tamil?
qa.a: The owner was delighted, probably feeling respected by his effort to learn the local language.

grounding: Shows a young man over months adapting to a new city while keeping his home traditions.

passage: Mohit beta, you're leaving for Canada next month, so let me, your Rekha-bua, tell you something. I went to London at twenty-three as a nurse. The first year, I hid my accent and never brought dal to work because someone once wrinkled their nose. I felt like half a person. Then an older Jamaican nurse told me, "Bring your food. We'll trade." She taught me her patties, I taught her rajma. Slowly I stopped hiding. I made English friends, joined the choir at the hospital, but kept my Sunday phone calls home and my Diwali lamps. You don't have to become someone else to belong. Take what's good there, and keep what's good in you.

qa.q: What did Rekha teach the Jamaican nurse to cook?
qa.a: She taught her rajma.

qa.q: What did Rekha mean by feeling 'like half a person'?
qa.a: She felt self-conscious and incomplete, hiding parts of herself like her accent and her dal, so she didn't feel whole.

qa.q: What advice does Rekha give Mohit before he leaves?
qa.a: Take what's good in the new country and keep what's good in himself, without becoming someone else.

qa.q: How might the Jamaican nurse have seen Rekha's food?
qa.a: She saw it as something to share and trade, not something strange.

grounding: Shows an elder passing on how she adapted abroad while preserving identity and building belonging.

passage:
Dhruv's first Diwali in Rotterdam came with sideways rain and a cancelled tram.
He had planned it carefully: diyas bought from an Indian grocery two towns away, his mother's besan laddoo recipe on a voice note, and an invitation to Manoj's flat. Manoj was the only other Indian on his team and had lived there four years.
Now he stood under a bus shelter with a box of half-set laddoos going soft in the damp. For a moment he missed Jaipur so sharply it felt like hunger: the noise, the rooftops, his cousins lighting sparklers too close to the curtains.
He almost went home. Instead he texted Manoj, "Running late, still coming," and walked the whole way.
At the flat were Manoj, two Dutch colleagues and a Brazilian neighbour, all trying to light diyas at an open window. Dhruv laughed and showed them how to shield the flame.

qa.q: Why was Dhruv stuck at the bus shelter?
qa.a: His tram had been cancelled in the heavy rain.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he thought of Jaipur?
qa.a: A strong homesickness; he missed the noise, the rooftops and his cousins so much it felt like hunger.

qa.q: What helped Dhruv build belonging instead of going home?
qa.a: He kept his plan with Manoj and walked there, bringing his own festival to share with the new people he met.

qa.q: What might the evening be like for the Dutch colleagues and the neighbour?
qa.a: It was probably new and fun for them, and Dhruv showing them how to shield the flame let them join in rather than just watch 🎉

grounding: Shows a young migrant feeling nostalgia abroad yet keeping his festival and sharing it to build belonging in the new place.

passage:
Jagdish had lived in the Pune housing society for three months before anyone knew his name. In Kolkata, his whole para knew what he ate for breakfast.
He kept the things he couldn't give up: Sunday fish curry, even though rohu at the local market was expensive; Bengali songs while he ironed his shirts. But he'd stopped greeting people in the lift, embarrassed by his slow Marathi.
One evening Preeti from the fourth floor knocked because his music was coming through the wall. He apologised at once. She shook her head. "No, no. My mother used to sing this one. Can you send me the name?"
The next week she invited him to the society's Ganpati cleaning crew. He went, got paint on his only good kurta, and learnt the Marathi word for broom.
He still called his mother every Sunday at lunch. Now he had things to tell her.

qa.q: Why did Preeti knock on Jagdish's door?
qa.a: His music was coming through the wall.

qa.q: Why had Jagdish stopped greeting people in the lift?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about his slow Marathi.

qa.q: What could Jagdish keep doing to belong while staying himself?
qa.a: He could keep his Sunday fish curry and Bengali songs while saying yes to invitations like the cleaning crew and practising Marathi bit by bit.

qa.q: What is it like for Jagdish's mother when he calls now?
qa.a: She probably hears a happier son with new stories, which may ease any worry about him being alone in Pune.

grounding: Shows a young man in a new city holding on to his food, music and language while slowly finding belonging with neighbours.

passage:
"I cried in the supermarket today," Afreen admitted, dropping onto a kitchen chair in their Berlin flat. "Over coriander. They sell it in these tiny sad bunches."
Tenzin laughed, not unkindly. "Month three?"
"Month four."
"Month four is the worst. I cried over momo wrappers."
"How long did it last?"
"Until I stopped trying to be either fully German or fully from Dharamshala." Tenzin put the kettle on. "I joined a climbing club with Germans. And I found three Tibetan families who do Losar together. Both."
"I don't know anyone."
"You know me. And the Indian grocery near the U-Bahn has proper coriander on Fridays."
Afreen smiled weakly. "You're joking."
"Never joke about coriander." Tenzin handed her a mug. "Eid's next month. Invite people. Germans, Indians, whoever. Make your Ammi's sheer khurma."
"In this tiny kitchen?"
"Especially in this tiny kitchen."

qa.q: What made Afreen cry in the supermarket?
qa.a: Coriander sold in tiny sad bunches.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling in month four?
qa.a: Afreen felt homesick and lonely, crying over small reminders of home.

qa.q: How did Tenzin build belonging, and what does Tenzin suggest to Afreen?
qa.a: Tenzin joined a local climbing club and a Tibetan community; for Afreen, Tenzin suggests an Eid meal with guests of all backgrounds, keeping her identity while making connections.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Afreen's tears?
qa.a: Tenzin sees them as a normal stage, having cried over momo wrappers too, and responds with warmth and practical tips.

grounding: A flatmate who adapted to Berlin helps a homesick young woman build belonging without losing her identity.

passage: When I, Suraj, moved from Patna to Singapore for work, I thought the hard part would be the job. It was the silence. Nobody on my floor talked in the lift. At the office, people ate lunch at their desks. I missed shouting across the lane to my neighbour. For months I was polite and invisible. Aparna, my wife, joined me in the second year and changed things. She said good morning to the cleaner, Auntie Lim, who turned out to have a son studying in Chennai. She found the Bihari association that celebrated Chhath at the beach, with thekua and everything. I went reluctantly and stood waist-deep in the sea at sunrise, holding the soop, among forty families from home. I cried a bit. Back at work, I joined a colleague's Friday lunch group, learned their jokes, and taught them the word "jugaad". I'm both now. Some days it tires me. Most days it feels like more.

qa.q: What did the Bihari association celebrate at the beach?
qa.a: Chhath.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling in the first months in Singapore?
qa.a: Suraj felt lonely and invisible, missing the noise and closeness of home.

qa.q: What helped Suraj adapt while keeping his identity?
qa.a: Aparna's small friendly contacts, finding the Bihari association for Chhath, and joining a colleague's lunch group.

qa.q: How might Auntie Lim see Aparna's greetings?
qa.a: Auntie Lim probably felt noticed and warmed, which is how they found a connection through her son in Chennai.

grounding: A young man looks back on adapting to life in Singapore while keeping his Bihari identity through community.

passage: Buddy programme note, Ward 7, Auckland. Vinita (nurse, arrived from Kochi in February) is settling well clinically but told me in week six that she felt "like a guest in someone else's house". She is quieter at handovers than she was at interview, and apologises a lot. Madhuri, another nurse from India who came five years ago, offered to meet her for coffee on days off. Madhuri told her what had helped: learning the local slang, joining the hospital netball team, and finding the Malayali church group on Sundays, where she could speak her own language and eat familiar food. Vinita has now joined both. At last week's handover she politely corrected a doctor on a medication time and didn't apologise. I have encouraged her to go ahead with her idea of an Onam sadya for the ward lunch. — Kate, charge nurse

qa.q: When did Vinita arrive from Kochi?
qa.a: In February.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling in week six?
qa.a: Vinita felt lonely and unsure, like a guest in someone else's house, which made her quiet and over-apologetic.

qa.q: What balance helped Vinita settle?
qa.a: Joining local life, like the netball team, while keeping her language and food through the Malayali church group.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel helping Vinita?
qa.a: Madhuri probably felt glad to share what had helped her five years earlier, remembering how hard the start was.

grounding: A charge nurse's note shows a young migrant nurse in New Zealand building belonging while keeping her culture.

passage:
Berlin, 6 December

First real winter. The sun sets at 3.50 p.m. and I've been eating instant rice in my room and scrolling photos of Durga Puja from home. I missed it this year. I missed Ma's shukto. I missed noise.

Today in German class, Gopika, from Kerala, asked if I wanted to go to the Indian grocery in Wedding. We bought mustard oil and posto and spent the tram ride complaining about the cold.

Then she dragged me to the Saturday language café, where Germans practise English and we practise German. I said "Ich bin Anirban" and a retired man named Klaus laughed kindly and corrected my grammar.

I don't want to become someone who only eats rice and talks to Bengalis. I also don't want to become someone who forgets posto.

So: German class Tuesday and Thursday. Language café Saturday. And next Sunday I'm cooking posto for Gopika, Klaus, and anyone else who comes.

qa.q: Where did Anirban and Gopika go shopping?
qa.a: They went to the Indian grocery in Wedding.

qa.q: How was Anirban feeling before the trip with Gopika?
qa.a: Anirban felt homesick and lonely, eating instant rice in the room and looking at photos of Durga Puja.

qa.q: What balance does Anirban plan between old identity and new belonging?
qa.a: Anirban plans to keep going to German class and the language café while cooking posto for new friends, holding on to home while building ties.

qa.q: How might Klaus see Anirban at the language café?
qa.a: Klaus seems kind and amused, happy to help a newcomer and perhaps curious to taste the posto.

grounding: A young adult in a new country misses home, keeps cultural roots and builds belonging through language and shared food.

passage:
The rural hospital in Wai had one nurse from the north-east: Lalremsiami, who had arrived from Aizawl in June. Everyone called her "sister", and nobody could pronounce her name.

The first months were hard. The food was too spicy, the Marathi fast. At night she called her mother and pretended everything was good.

Madhuri, the ward nurse she shared shifts with, noticed her eating plain rice from a tiffin every day. One afternoon she said, "Teach me one Mizo dish, and I'll teach you to make pohe without chilli."

In September, Madhuri invited her home for Ganpati. Lalremsiami brought bai, a Mizo stew, and Madhuri's aunt asked for the recipe.

Lalremsiami still went to the small church in town every Sunday, and still sang in Mizo on night shifts when the ward was quiet. But now, when the ward boy mispronounced her name, Madhuri corrected him: "Lal-rem-sia-mi. Say it properly."

qa.q: Which festival did Madhuri invite Lalremsiami home for?
qa.a: Madhuri invited her home for Ganpati.

qa.q: How was Lalremsiami feeling in her first months in Wai?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt homesick and lonely, struggling with the food and language and pretending to her mother that everything was fine.

qa.q: How did Madhuri help Lalremsiami belong without asking her to give up her identity?
qa.a: Madhuri offered a food exchange, invited her to Ganpati, and made others say her name properly, while Lalremsiami kept her church and songs.

qa.q: How might Madhuri's aunt see Lalremsiami after tasting the bai?
qa.a: The aunt seems curious and warm towards her, which shows that sharing her culture helped her be welcomed.

grounding: A young nurse from Mizoram adapts to a small town in Maharashtra, building belonging while keeping her faith, language and food.

passage:
Olga moved from Kraków to Dublin at twenty-four for a job in a software firm. The first winter was grey and lonely. She ate dinner at her desk and video-called her mother every night, crying sometimes after she hung up.
Christmas Eve was the worst. At home, it meant Wigilia: twelve dishes, an empty chair for a stranger, the whole family. In Dublin, her flatmates had gone home.
Her colleague Hana, from Osaka, was alone too. On an impulse, Olga invited her. They cooked a small Wigilia together: pierogi, beetroot soup, poppy-seed cake. Hana brought mochi. Olga explained the empty chair, and they laughed that Hana was the stranger.
Next year Olga did it again, with six people from four countries. She still missed Kraków. But now she had a tradition of her own in the new city, built from the old one.

qa.q: What did Hana bring to the Christmas Eve dinner?
qa.a: Mochi.

qa.q: How did Olga feel during her first winter in Dublin?
qa.a: Olga felt lonely and homesick, eating alone and sometimes crying after calls with her mother.

qa.q: How did Olga preserve her identity while building belonging?
qa.a: She adapted her home tradition, Wigilia, and shared it with others far from home, making it a new tradition in Dublin.

qa.q: How might Hana have felt being invited as the stranger?
qa.a: Hana probably felt touched and included, sharing her own food while learning Olga's tradition.

grounding: Shows a young adult adapting to a new country by sharing a home tradition to build belonging.

passage:
At the newcomer centre in Toronto, Gurleen sat across from Reena, a settlement counsellor who'd come from Ludhiana herself fifteen years earlier.
Gurleen was twenty-five, three months in, working night shifts in a warehouse despite her commerce degree. "I thought I'd feel excited," she said. "Mostly I feel invisible."
Reena didn't give a speech. She asked what Gurleen missed most. "Speaking Punjabi without thinking. Gurdwara on Sundays. Being someone."
They made a plan. A free course to get her degree assessed and a bridging programme in accounting. A Sunday visit to the gurdwara near her room. And a conversation group at the centre, where newcomers practised Canadian workplace English and shared tips.
"You don't have to choose between the old you and the new place," Reena said. "You add."
Gurleen left with three flyers and, for the first time in weeks, something like energy.

qa.q: Where was Gurleen working?
qa.a: Night shifts in a warehouse.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel three months after arriving?
qa.a: Gurleen felt invisible and disappointed, not excited as she had expected.

qa.q: What did Reena's plan do to help Gurleen adapt while keeping her identity?
qa.a: It combined steps to rebuild her career with the gurdwara and Punjabi connection and a newcomer group for belonging.

qa.q: How might Reena feel helping someone from her own home region?
qa.a: Reena probably feels empathy and warmth, remembering her own hard start fifteen years earlier.

grounding: Illustrates a young migrant adapting to a new country with support while preserving her identity.

passage:
Dear Indu,
You asked how Dubai is after one year. Honestly? Better now. It wasn't at first.
For the first months I only worked and slept. The heat, the rules, the speed of everything. I felt like a guest who didn't know where anything was kept. I also felt guilty for missing home when I'd been so eager to leave.
Things that helped: I joined a Malayalam association that meets on Fridays, so I speak our language and eat Amma's kind of fish curry. I also joined a running group with people from ten countries, which made me learn how others do things. My colleague from Egypt taught me how to be polite in Arabic.
I still call Amma every night. I still miss the rain in Kochi. But I don't feel like a guest anymore. More like someone with two homes.
Your brother,
Deepak

qa.q: What day does the Malayalam association meet?
qa.a: On Fridays.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel during the first months in Dubai?
qa.a: Deepak felt lost and guilty, like a guest who didn't know where anything was kept.

qa.q: How did Deepak build belonging while keeping his identity?
qa.a: Deepak joined a Malayalam association to keep language and food, and a mixed running group to learn from others.

qa.q: How might Indu feel reading that her brother feels he has two homes?
qa.a: Indu would probably feel relieved and happy, though she may still miss him.

grounding: Shows a young migrant adapting to a new city while preserving personal identity and building belonging.

passage: Jagdish Uncle, you asked what the first year in Melbourne was really like. The first winter I cried in the supermarket because I couldn't find the right dal and everything smelled wrong. At work I laughed too loudly and apologised too much. I nearly booked a ticket home in July. What helped was doing two things at once. I joined a Sunday bushwalking group, full of people who had nothing to do with India, and made myself say yes to the barbecues, even when I didn't know the rules. And I found the gurdwara in Craigieburn, where the aunties feed everyone and nobody asks why you've come. Now I cook rajma for my colleagues on Fridays and they bring me lamingtons. I still miss Amritsar in my stomach when it rains. But I, Ishita, am not a visitor here anymore. I think I'm both.

qa.q: What does Ishita cook for colleagues on Fridays?
qa.a: Ishita cooks rajma for them.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel during the first winter?
qa.a: Ishita felt homesick and out of place, crying in the supermarket and nearly booking a ticket home.

qa.q: What helped Ishita adapt without losing identity?
qa.a: Joining a local bushwalking group and saying yes to barbecues, while also finding a gurdwara community and sharing home food at work.
